stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Sedition Act, 1798: it made it a crime to write, print, or publish false, scandalous, and malicious writings against the government of the United States, either house of Congress, or the president, with intent to defame them or bring them into contempt. James Madison, Virginia Resolution, December 1798: “In case of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of other powers, not granted by the said compact, the states who are parties thereto, have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil.”
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrased from the Sedition Act, July 14, 1798; James Madison, Virginia Resolution, December 24, 1798. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the Sedition Act, July 14, 1798, and quotes James Madison, Virginia Resolution, December 24, 1798, public domain.
stem: What was the main political result of the Alien and Sedition Acts?

options.text: The Federalists won every election for the next twenty years.
options.misconception: Background: the Federalists lost the election of 1800 and never won the presidency again.

options.text: The Supreme Court struck the acts down as unconstitutional at once.
options.misconception: Background: the Court did not rule on the acts, and they expired or were repealed instead.

options.text: The acts backfired: the Democratic-Republicans gained strength and won in 1800.
The Democratic-Republicans dissolved their party and joined the Federalists.
options.misconception: Background: the Democratic-Republicans grew stronger and won the election of 1800.

rationales.C: Background: voters saw the acts as an attack on free speech, and Jefferson won the presidency in 1800 while the Federalists never won it again.
rationales.A: The Federalists lost power after 1800 instead of winning every election.
rationales.B: The Court did not strike the acts down; that was not how they ended.
rationales.D: The Democratic-Republicans grew stronger, not weaker.
rationales.general:
1. The stimulus shows the acts punishing criticism of the government, and the resolutions answering them.
2. Background: voters saw the acts as an attack on free speech, and Jefferson won the presidency in 1800 while the Federalists never won it again.
3. A law meant to weaken the opposition instead gave it a cause and a martyr’s story.
4. So the main result was the opposite of what the Federalists intended: their rivals gained power.
Remember: a law that silences critics often hands them their best campaign issue.
